chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Black population of Homestead and the steel mills
summary: The Black community grew with migration from the South to work in the mills; ethnic mix of Hungarians and Poles; school segregation.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I just thought of something I wanted to ask you from before. You said your paternal grandmother was the first black person to settle in Homestead.
That's right.
Around, let's say, just before World War I, do you remember what proportion of the population would have been black at that time?

Well, let's see -- there were quite a few families -- in fact Chet Campbell's family was one of the original families to live in Homestead. I would say there might have been about ten or fifteen black families that would be the first families to live there.
Do you know how that came about? How they came to choose Homestead, is it because the steel mills were there?
Yeah, I would think it was on account of the mills. But of course at the outset of the War, there was what -- in those days they called it the transportation, but it was an influx

of blacks from the South to work in the mill because a lot of the younger people living there were called off to war.

Earl Hines depicts that I've just been reading the first few pages of the Stanley Dance book in which he talks about his days in Pittsburgh and he depicts that in almost a negative kind of a way. He says it brought about a lot of social dislocation. You know, previously it was kind of a stable --
Well, it would. I mean a lot of new people coming in --
And that's when segrega- tion really started in that area.
Possibly. Earl is a little older than I am. He probably can remember further back than I would remember.
He was born in 1905.
I wouldn't know. I wouldn't have paid much attention to it but I know when I went to school in the early days there were seldom any more than three or four black kids in the

class. In fact in the later grades, like 6th, 7th and 8th grades, I'd wind up in a class where there'd be only maybe one other black besides myself. And of course this was after World War I, but I don't know. I don't know that it --
There were something like a dozen or so black families before?
Yeah, black families there.
After World War I, how had that changed?

Well, because of the influx of more blacks there that would mean a larger proportion of blacks in the city. But I don't know just what effect this might have had -- what segregation or integration, whatever -- there were sections -- I suppose in any small -- where so-called poorer people lived than people who are more affluent. But as I recall the majority of the blacks and also some of the -- You know we, at the time, we had a lot of what we considered foreigners. Well, you say aliens had come to Homestead to work in

the mill. Hungarians, Slavic, Polish -- we had a few Jewish settlers, I imagine they might have been there they were more in the stable community. But we had a real influx of aliens who'd come to work in the mill. You must recall that this was the beginning of Andrew Carnegie steel mill in Homestead, so I'm pretty sure that the history books will state that they had settlers from all over, all over the European area.
Especially east Europe, yeah.
